title: Witnessed by the gods
hookLine: face to face at last, Nala questions Damayanti's faith, and a god answers for her
carry: a marriage is vowed with the gods as witness
last: HEARING A SACRED STORY IS A SHELTER.

cards: Nala and Damayanti are face to face at last, in her father's house, after the forest, the cut cloth, the long separation. He still wears the changed, unlovely shape that has hidden him.
And the hardest thing he says is a question for her: how could a faithful wife send out word that she'd choose another husband? The man who walked away is asking her to account for herself.
Her third choice: what to say to that.

teach.b: When she sees him, she speaks with grief and no softening: what kind of man leaves a sleeping wife alone in the forest? Nala tells her it wasn't fully him: Kali had been inside him, and now Kali is gone.
Then he asks his question. How could a faithful wife announce she'd choose again? Damayanti answers it straight.
It was never real. It was a way to bring him to Vidarbha, because only he could drive a king there in a single day.
And then she does what Hindu stories do with the deepest promises: she calls the gods to witness. In paraphrase: let the Wind, who moves through this whole world, take my life if I have done wrong.

teach.h: THE WIND SAYS SHE KEPT FAITH
teach.b: The Wind answers, a voice from the sky: she has kept faith with you the whole time. Only then does Nala put on the serpent's garment and become himself again. Here's the teaching.
A Hindu marriage isn't only an agreement between two people. It's a vow made in front of the gods. That's why, at a Hindu wedding, the couple walk around a sacred fire.

teach.h: AGNI SAKSHI: THE FIRE AS WITNESS
teach.b: Agni, the fire god, is the witness; Hindus say the vows are made agni sakshi, with the fire as witness. Agni was in the hall the day Damayanti chose Nala, and blessed them. Years later, the Wind spoke up for her.

teach.h: A MARRIAGE IS VOWED WITH THE GODS AS WITNESS.
teach.b: Many teachers read it this way: the gods who witness a vow also keep watch over it. So when you see a couple circling the fire, it isn't for the photos. Two people are asking a god to watch them keep their word.

how: Hindus know Nala and Damayanti's reunion from the Mahabharata's forest book; the sage tells it to Yudhishthira, who had also lost his kingdom at dice.

games.q: you're Damayanti. Nala doubts your faithfulness, and you have no proof. what do you do?
o: call the gods to witness: let the Wind take my life if I've done wrong.
say nothing; he'll believe you in time.
send him away for doubting you.
games.why: she calls on the gods to witness, and the Wind answers from the sky: she has kept faith the whole time.

practice: Bring to mind one promise you're keeping, to a partner, a friend, your family, yourself. Picture a small flame in front of you, the way a diya burns at a puja, and say the promise quietly to it, as if to a witness.
Breathe with it for a few breaths; you don't need to judge how well you've kept it. If you pray, you can ask God to keep watch over it.

wordCard.voice: Damayanti. The princess who chose the mortal, searched with a question, and kept a vow the Wind itself spoke up for.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the princess of Vidarbha, daughter of King Bhima, whose story Brihadashva tells in the Mahabharata's forest book.

carryVoice: Your line: a marriage is vowed with the gods as witness. For Damayanti, the Wind spoke up. Go gently.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Nalopakhyana (the reunion in Vidarbha: Damayanti's reproach; Nala on Kali; his question about the second swayamvara; her answer and her oath calling the Wind to witness; the Wind's voice; Karkotaka's garment)
